Article Title: Hack of the day: How to check your rooftop solar subsidy status
Article Text:
What it solves

What to do

Steps

Important note

Checking the status of your rooftop solar subsidy can often feel confusing, with applications moving through multiple stages of approval, installation, and financial processing. Many consumers lose track of where their request stands, leading to delays or uncertainty about when the subsidy will be credited. The government’s PM Surya Ghar app offers a simple solution by allowing applicants to monitor their rooftop solar journey in real time. From the moment you submit your application to the point where your subsidy is processed, the app provides clear updates on each stage. By signing in with your registered details, you can view your rooftop solar application, check its current status, and track progress until completion. While updates may depend on your DISCOM and required approvals, the app ensures you have a transparent view of the process. This digital tool makes subsidy tracking easier, faster, and more reliable for solar adopters.Many rooftop solar applicants lose track of their approvals, installation stages, and subsidy processing. Article Title: Apple left a video of its camera AirPods inside a Mac update, and this is what they look like
Article Text:
Apple demoed a camera you can't see, in a video it didn't mean to publish.

AirPods cameras are for Siri, not for you to click photos

A frame from the demo video Apple left in macOS 26.7, alongside a closer look at the bud. The stem is thicker than the AirPods Pro 3. (Image: MacRumors/Aaron Perris)

Apple employees have been wearing prototypes for months

A September launch could be on the table, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro

The first real look at Apple's camera AirPods didn't come from the usual suspects. It came from Apple, by mistake. Buried in the macOS Tahoe 26.7 release candidate that landed Monday is a short demo video showing a man wearing AirPods holding up a book, with a Siri voiceover explaining that Visual Intelligence makes "your world becomes savable" and that you can ask it to save what you're looking at for later. MacRumors found the clip.You have to look twice to spot what's different. The bud in the video could pass for an AirPods Pro 3. No visible lens, no sensor housing, just a stem that reads slightly thicker than the current one. MacRumors also found the release candidate littered with references to codename B790, including an error string about an image stream failing on the left bud. Elsewhere in the same build: a warning telling users to keep the AirPods uncovered so the system can read their surroundings accurately. Long hair, evidently, is a known problem.What the cameras actually do is narrower than it sounds. According to Bloomberg's Mark Gurman, they capture low-resolution visual information for Siri to reason about, not photos or video. Look at what's in your fridge, ask what to cook. Walk somewhere and get directions that account for what's in front of you.The demo fits that description. Nobody takes a picture in it. A man looks at a book, Siri saves the book, and that is the whole feature.Gurman has also described longer stems and an LED that lights up when visual data goes to the cloud. Neither turns up in the video.Apple testers have been using prototypes daily since at least May, Bloomberg reported at the time, at the design validation test stage. That is the step immediately before production validation, which means the physical design is locked and what follows is a manufacturing problem rather than a product one. Everything after DVT is about yields and tooling. It also explains why the software looks finished. A team that far along has hardware stable enough to build onboarding screens against, which is exactly what turned up in macOS this week.Earlier this month, Bloomberg reported that camera AirPods could arrive as soon as this year, pulling forward a device most people had penciled in for 2027. Apple's iPhone event is expected in early September, where the iPhone 18 Pro, 18 Pro Max and the first foldable iPhone are due.One wrinkle worth keeping straight: B790 is not the camera AirPods Gurman has been writing about since 2025. That model, B798, slipped to 2027 after Apple's Siri delays. B790 is a separate project that got there first.Apple, as usual, hasn't confirmed any of it. But a release candidate is the last build before public release, and this one already has setup screens and error messages for the thing. That normally means the hardware is done. September will tell us the rest.
Article Summary: AirPods cameras are for Siri, not for you to click photos. The bud in the video could pass for an AirPods Pro 3. Apple employees have been wearing prototypes for months. A September launch could be on the table, alongside the iPhone 18 Pro.

Article Title: In 2005 for the first time, scientists documented giant squid in their natural habitat, since then many mysteries about their lives remain in ...
Article Text:
A diorama unlike any other in the museum

The real-life battle behind the display

Decades of mystery, only recently interrupted

An unassuming black box near the American Museum of Natural History's iconic blue whale draws in unsuspecting visitors to one of the museum's most striking exhibits, according to a Popular Science report. Every few seconds, a light flashes inside an otherwise pitch-black display, briefly revealing a row of sharp teeth and reddish tentacles as a sperm whale clamps down on a giant squid. The Sperm Whale and Giant Squid Diorama offers a rare, dramatic glimpse into one of the ocean's most mysterious predator-prey relationships, one that scientists are still working to fully understand.Unlike most of AMNH's other displays, this diorama has no glass front. Instead, its dark, reflective interior creates a mirror-like effect that reportedly confused early visitors into thinking the exhibit was empty. The darkness isn't incidental, it's designed to recreate the lightless conditions of the deep ocean, where sunlight never reaches.That same design also makes the diorama unusually labor-intensive to clean. In a video recently shared on social media, AMNH Exhibition Maintenance staffer Janet Spiller can be seen using a backpack vacuum fitted with fiber pole attachments to reach into the exhibit's nooks and crannies, a job that can take a single person up to four hours to complete.The scene depicted in the diorama reflects a genuine and extreme biological encounter. Sperm whales (Physeter macrocephalus) are known to dive more than 6,500 feet, a depth equivalent to stacking roughly four and a half Empire State Buildings on top of one another, and can remain submerged for over 60 minutes at a time in pursuit of giant squid (Architeuthis dux).Much of what scientists know about this underwater clash comes from indirect evidence rather than direct observation. Sperm whales are sometimes found with circular marks on their skin, believed to be sucker marks left behind from squid fighting to escape. Researchers have also recovered giant squid beaks, the hard biting structures used by the animal, inside the stomachs of sperm whales, offering further proof of these deep-sea encounters.Despite the drama depicted in exhibits like this one, giant squid remain one of the ocean's most elusive animals. Scientists did not document a giant squid in its natural habitat on camera until 2005, and even now, many aspects of the species' life in the deep ocean remain largely unknown. The persistence of that mystery is part of what continues to make the predator-prey relationship between sperm whales and giant squid such a compelling subject for both researchers and museum visitors alike.
Article Summary: The Sperm Whale and Giant Squid Diorama offers a rare, dramatic glimpse into one of the ocean's most mysterious predator-prey relationships. Unlike most of AMNH's other displays, this diorama has no glass front. Its dark, reflective interior creates a mirror-like effect that reportedly confused early visitors into thinking the exhibit was empty.

Article Title: BoatStone 900 Bluetooth speaker review: The party speaker that punches well above its price
Article Text:
Rating: 3.5/5

Design

Features and performance

Battery

Verdict

Let's be clear about what the Stone 900 is trying to be. It's not chasing the audiophile crowd, and it's not pretending to be a sleek minimalist desk speaker either. This is a party speaker, full stop — big, loud, covered in RGB lights, and priced at Rs 5,999 to make it an easy impulse buy before a weekend gathering. boAt is promising 80W of output, the ability to pair two units together for stereo sound, and up to 15 hours of battery. So does it actually deliver. We used this latest Bluetooth speaker from Boat to see how it performs.You're not sneaking this into a backpack. At 372 x 152 x 201 mm, the Stone 900 has real heft and presence — it's built for a tabletop, a tailgate, or the floor next to a cooler, not a commute. It comes in two colourways, Graphite Black and a more outdoorsy Jungle Terrain, and Boattosses in a matching silicone cover along with the USB-C cable, manual and warranty card in the box. Nothing about the build screams luxury, and honestly, it shouldn't. This is a speaker that's going to get knocked over, splashed on, and dragged from the living room to the backyard, and the design leans into that reality rather than fighting it. The IPX5 rating backs that up — it'll shrug off a splash or a sweaty hand without drama, which matters more here than a nicer finish would.For the price, Boat has packed in a genuinely solid feature list.The 80W output comes from a combination of dual 1-inch tweeters and dual 3.5-inch full-range drivers, a pairing that's meant to keep the highs from getting harsh while giving the low end enough muscle to fill a yard.The feature that actually changes how you'd use this speaker, though, is TWS pairing. Link two Stone 900 units together and you get proper stereo separation plus double the output — suddenly this isn't just "a speaker," it's the backbone of an actual outdoor sound system. Connectivity is sensible too: Bluetooth 5.3 covers wireless streaming, but there's AUX and USB on hand as a backup, so a dead Bluetooth connection or a phone that's run out of juice doesn't kill the party. Then there's the stuff that sounds minor on paper but matters in practice — hands-free calling through the built-in mic, direct access to your phone's voice assistant, and RGB lighting that pulses along with whatever's playing. That last one, if we're honest, is doing more heavy lifting for the "party speaker" vibe than most people will admit.Performance is where the Stone 900 earns its keep, or doesn't, and for the most part, it earns it. Throw on something bass-heavy like Kesariya or Kala Chashma and the dual 3.5-inch drivers do exactly what you'd want at a gathering — there's real low-end thump, not the thin, boxy rattle you get from cheaper "party speakers" that talk a big game and deliver none of it. Same goes for high-energy English tracks like Blinding Lights or Uptown Funk — both lean on punchy bass and forward percussion, which plays right into how this speaker is tuned. Where it's a little less impressive is with more delicate, vocal-first material. Something like Tum Hi Ho or a quieter acoustic ballad still sounds fine, perfectly listenable, but you won't get the same separation or subtlety you'd hear on a speaker tuned for accuracy rather than impact. That's not really a flaw so much as a trade-off — this speaker was built to win a backyard, not a critical listening session, and it's honest about that.Worth repeating: pairing two units in TWS mode isn't just a volume boost, it genuinely widens the stereo image, and that difference is much more noticeable on dance and pop tracks with wide, layered production than it is on something stripped-down and vocal-heavy.Boatquotes up to 15 hours on a charge, and like pretty much every Bluetooth speaker on the market, that number assumes you're not blasting it at full volume the entire time. Push the Stone 900 hard at a party and you'll see that number drop noticeably, so if you're planning an all-day outdoor event, it's worth having the charger within reach rather than assuming you're covered. Speaking of which, charging happens over USB-C and takes 4 to 5 hours for a full top-up, which isn't blazing fast by 2026 standards, but it's not unusual for a speaker in this size and price bracket either.For what it costs, the Stone 900 makes a pretty compelling case for itself. It's loud, it's got real bass, it can handle a splash without panic, and the TWS pairing option means it can genuinely scale up if you want to go bigger than a single unit. If what you actually want is something to throw on for a backyard hangout, a road trip, or a evening with friends where the goal is volume and vibe over audiophile nuance, the Stone 900 gets the job done
Article Summary: At 372 x 152 x 201 mm, the Stone 900 has real heft and presence. It's built for a tabletop, a tailgate, or the floor next to a cooler, not a commute. It comes in two colourways, Graphite Black and a more outdoorsy Jungle Terrain.

Article Title: Netflix unveils ‘VOID’, an AI model that can change a movie plot
Article Text:
Netflix

How Netflix VOID works







Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. Most object-removal technology leaves a gap where something used to be and/ or fills it with a plausible-looking background. VOID goes a step further: after erasing an object from a scene, it calculates how the surrounding environment should realistically respond to its absence, and in the process it adjusts the behaviour of other elements in the frame accordingly.The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness that sets it apart from several existing tools.For example, imagine this scenario: A movie director has just wrapped up a multi-million dollar action sequence where the star drives straight into a fiery, head-on collision. The cars explode, debris scatters, and the scene is a wrap.But suddenly, there is request to change the scene: The character survives and drive off into the sunset instead. This would mean costly reshoots or millions spent on computer-generated graphics.Netflix’s VOID can alter the scene and digitally erase the collision, the second vehicle, the smoke, and the flying debris. It will then generate new, realistic footage of pristine pavement, making it look as though the main character simply drove down an empty, peaceful road.The AI’s ‘magic’ lies in its grasp of real-world physics. Let us understand this by a different example. If a video shows a person jumping into a pool and splashing water onto the deck, VOID can completely erase the person. It will then intelligently alter the water and the wet concrete, leaving behind a perfectly still, undisturbed pool as if nobody had ever jumped in.“To train the model, we generate a new paired dataset of counterfactual object removals using Kubric and HUMOTO, where removing an object requires altering downstream physical interactions. During inference, a vision-language model identifies regions of the scene affected by the removed object. These regions are then used to guide a video diffusion model that generates physically consistent counterfactual outcomes,” Netflix said.“Experiments on both synthetic and real data show that our approach better preserves consistent scene dynamics after object removal compared to prior video object removal methods,” the company added.Netflix isn’t keeping this powerful tool locked behind studio doors, and made the VOID model available to the public on the AI platform Hugging Face, allowing anyone to download and use it.While there are already several video-altering tools on the market, such as Runway, DiffuEraser, and ProPainter, the Netflix team claims VOID is vastly superior, as per The Register.
Article Summary: Netflix has unveiled an AI model that can alter the scene. While this is nothing new, Netflix’s model not just remove objects from video, it understands what should happen next, essentially altering the causality. The model, called VOID, is a vision-language system designed to edit video footage with a level of contextual awareness.

Article Title: Analogue paneer, cockroaches: FDA crackdown hits Bandra's Otters Club, Zepto warehouse, 4 others in Mumbai
Article Text:
Mumbai's Food and Drug Administration has suspended licenses for several establishments





MUMBAI: The Food and Drug Administration (FDA) has cracked down on yet another club after initial five elite clubs and gymkhanas had their food license suspended. This time, severe hygiene violations were found at Otters Club on Carter Road in Bandra. There was also another Zepto warehouse which had its license suspended.At the upscale Otters, inspections showed broken tiles, blocked drains, malfunctioning refrigerator with volatile temperature fluctuations. It was noted that the flooring was unclean in certain areas and records of Total Polar Compounds (TPC) testing in edible oil were missing.Inspectors also discovered that the club's restaurant was serving analogue paneer to its customers by using product named "regular paneer" supplied by Punjab Sind Dairy.Simultaneously, authorities clamped down on online delivery platform Zepto's Chembur facility on the Eastern Express Highway. They found temperature control failures where meat items were stored; it was 9 degrees Celsius instead of the mandated 5 degrees or below, and frozen items sat at minus 11 degrees instead of the required minus 18 degrees or lower.The Chembur dark store also had greasy, slippery floors, accumulated black dust on exhaust fans, poor ventilation, and an overall lack of cleaning schedules that fostered conditions for cockroaches and pests.Four other food businesses had their license suspended in the city. One was in Dahisar, where according to FDA officials, Daily Fresh Bakers and Cakes in Dahisar had been preparing cakes directly on unclean kitchen floors with active cockroach and ant infestations.Similarly, Prince of Wales Restaurant in Khar faced suspension over poor temperature controls, lack of pest control measures, and a lack of proper cleaning of equipment. Raj Oil Trading in Vile Parle had rat-bite marks on its oil packets and foul odours from poorly maintained storage, while Cafe Sifarish in Andheri East was also shut down following lapses in hygiene.
Article Summary: Mumbai's Food and Drug Administration has suspended licenses for several establishments. The initial five elite clubs and gymkhanas had their food license suspended. This time, severe hygiene violations were found at Otters Club in Bandra. Four other food businesses had their license suspended in the city.

Article Title: Kirloskar Vasundhara Film Festival returns with in-person edition
Article Text:
(From left) Consultant SL Kirloskar CSR Foundation Suresh Mijar, foundation CEO Jagdish Purandare, director Arti Kirloskar, co-founder of The Youth Cosmo Nidhi Bennur and director of Ecological Society Kedar Bhagwat at a press conference announcing the festival

Pune:





The Kirloskar Vasundhara International Film Festival (KVIFF) returns to an in-person format for its 19th edition, bringing together films, discussions, performances and community activities around environmental issues.The festival has been organised by the SL Kirloskar CSR Foundation and will be held on Aug 21-22 at the Pune International Centre, Pashan. This year’s theme is Brought to You by Earth and aims to encourage people to pay close attention to the changing climate, fragile ecosystems and the environment.The annual festival began in 2007 as a platform to build environmental awareness through cinema and public engagement. It moved online during the Covid-19 pandemic in 2020. This year, it returns to a physical venue with a programme designed for Kirloskar Group employees, students of Kirloskar schools and the wider community.The first day is exclusively curated for Kirloskar Group employees. “We want to inculcate a regard for the environment into our employees as well as the wider community. Ideas and concepts emerging over the previous editions have been incorporated into our daily functions — like becoming a zero-waste organisation,” said director of SL Kirloskar CSR Foundation Arti Kirloskar.Kirloskar said that following last year’s theme Healthy Society, Nutritious Food and Flourishing Nature, the organisation had introduced several changes. “Our canteen serves mainly millet dishes, along with promoting clean eating and other sustainable practices,” she said.The second day will begin with a special session for students of CB Tube Sadhana Kanya Vidyalay, Loyola High School and St Joseph High School at 9am. “The schools are close to the venue, so we have coordinated with them. Hopefully, other schools will want to participate in future editions. The goal is to increasingly get students to attend and take part,” she said.The student programme will include two short-film screenings, interactive discussions and a workshop aimed to make environmental issues easy for young audiences to understand.Nidhi Bennur of The Youth Cosmo, a social enterprise that works with young people on environmental awareness, will conduct two sessions. One will explore pastoral communities in India, while the other will look at the migration of animals and humans. The latter session will examine why migration happens and how it is connected to larger ecological systems.“The goal is to help children see themselves as part of larger ecological systems and consider how their individual actions can contribute to environmental stewardship,” said Bennur.The evening programme will include Ghungroo — a folk dance performance by the Melghat tribal community. It will be followed by three environment-related short films and a feature film curated by ALT EFF. A student-led skit will also be presented.The festival will conclude with the Vasundhara Sanman and Vasundhara Mitra awards, which recognise individuals and organisations for their contribution to environmental protection. An eco-bazaar will also be held from 3pm to 7.30pm, featuring sustainable products, innovations and community-led initiatives.
Article Summary: The Kirloskar Vasundhara International Film Festival returns to an in-person format for its 19th edition. This year’s theme is Brought to You by Earth and aims to encourage people to pay close attention to the changing climate, fragile ecosystems and the environment.

Article Title: Real-time management: AI-powered platform planned to help track crowds, simulate scenarios & strengthen emergency response during Kumbh
Article Text:
Smart City corporation's command-and-control room, fully equipped and operational for the Kumbh Mela

Nashik

:





The Nashik-Trimbakeshwar Kumbh Mela Authority (NTKMA) will deploy an AI-powered “Digital Twin” platform for crowd control, mobility planning, emergency response, and disaster preparedness at the Simhastha Kumbh Mela 2027, strengthening technology-led event management.The proposed system will create a live digital replica of the Kumbh ecosystem by integrating GIS-based 2D and 3D maps with real-time operational data, surveillance feeds and AI analytics. Officials said the platform would serve as a decision-support tool, enabling authorities to monitor ground conditions, assess risks and coordinate multiple agencies involved in managing the event.Built on Integrated Command and Control Centre (ICCC), ‘Digital Twin’ will function as a unified dashboard for departments handling crowd management, traffic, sanitation, health services, security, disaster management and public amenities. “The platform will continuously process data from multiple sources to provide a real-time view of the Kumbh environment. Authorities will be able to track crowd density, analyse movement patterns, generate alerts and assess operational challenges as they emerge. It will also allow officials to simulate scenarios and evaluate response strategies before implementation,” an official said.Crowd intelligence and public safety are expected to be among its key applications.“By analysing pedestrian movement and crowd concentrations across bathing ghats, temples, roads and transit hubs, officials will be able to identify bottlenecks and prevent congestion during peak pilgrimage days,” the official said.It will also support transport planning by integrating traffic flows, public transport operations, parking facilities and pedestrian movement into a single digital framework. Officials said this would help improve diversion plans, optimise resource deployment and strengthen mobility management.Beyond crowd and traffic monitoring, 'Digital Twin’ will cover health services, emergency response, sanitation and waste management, utility services, environmental and river monitoring, weather-risk assessment and disaster preparedness. It will also assist in workforce deployment, lost-and-found operations and citizen support services.“The initiative is part of the proposed Maha Simhastha Kumbh AI Stack, which also includes an AI-first call centre, AI-powered lost-and-found services and ‘KumbhDoot’, an AI-based virtual assistant for pilgrims,” another official said.The digital ecosystem is proposed to be integrated with the Kumbh website and mobile application, offering crowd-density heat maps, route guidance, SOS support, weather alerts, traffic updates, parking information and public facility details.NTKMA commissioner Shekhar Singh said 'Digital Twin’ would operate on a “human-in-the-loop” model, with AI-generated insights supporting rather than replacing administrative decision-making. “It will operate on a human-in-the-loop model, with intelligent automation complemented by human oversight and validation. The objective is to use technology to strengthen the capacity of officials and field agencies to anticipate situations, assess alternatives and take timely decisions,” Singh said.With millions of pilgrims expected to attend Simhastha Kumbh Mela 2027, authorities believe the platform will improve safety, operational efficiency and service delivery while enabling more coordinated, data-driven management of one of the world’s largest religious gatherings.
Article Summary: The Nashik-Trimbakeshwar Kumbh Mela Authority (NTKMA) will deploy an AI-powered ‘Digital Twin’ platform for crowd control, mobility planning, emergency response, and disaster preparedness. The proposed system will integrate GIS- based 2D and 3D maps with real-time operational data, surveillance feeds and AI analytics.

Article Title: Meet Meghana Addanki, the 17-year-old New Jersey student who turned eggshells and cotton into a tiny generator that harvests energy from movement
Article Text:
Image AI generated

How eggshell membrane and cotton were modified with zinc oxide for energy harvesting

Eggshell membrane and mercerised cotton form a 5 by 3 centimetre hybrid nanogenerator

Meghana Addanki’s hybrid nanogenerator reaches 33.29 volts during forceful finger tapping

How Meghana Addanki’s natural-material generator could support wearable and portable electronics

At 17, Meghana Addanki was looking at two materials that would rarely be associated with electricity: eggshell membrane and cotton. The New Jersey high school student used both in an experiment designed to turn ordinary movement into usable electrical energy, developing a small hybrid generator with the help of zinc oxide. Her project brought together piezoelectric and triboelectric effects, allowing the device to respond when it was pressed, tapped or otherwise subjected to mechanical force. The finished generator measured just 5 by 3 centimetres, yet produced considerably higher voltages than the individual material-based components tested during the research. In one test, forceful finger tapping generated a peak of 33.29 volts, while the device reached a power density of 26.4 microwatts per square centimetre. Presented at ISEF 2025, Addanki's work explored whether natural, readily available materials could have a practical role in small-scale energy harvesting. The project also addressed a broader challenge in energy harvesting: finding materials that are inexpensive, flexible and less environmentally problematic than some conventional alternatives. By combining biological materials with zinc oxide, Addanki demonstrated a compact approach that could potentially power low-energy sensors or other small electronic devices.The unusual starting point for Addanki's project was the thin membrane found inside an eggshell. Eggshells themselves are familiar household waste, but the membrane has a different composition and structure. In her project, it was used as the base material for one part of the generator. Cotton, meanwhile, formed the upper section, giving the device two biomaterial components with different electrical characteristics.According to the project description published by the Society for Science, both materials were treated with zinc oxide (ZnO), with the amount varied between 10 and 30 per cent by weight. The aim was not simply to make the materials conductive. The modified biomaterials were tested as piezoelectric nanogenerators, devices that can produce an electrical response when mechanical strain is applied. At the highest ZnO concentration tested, the cotton-based component produced a peak voltage of 7.55 volts, while the eggshell-membrane component reached 7.10 volts.Addanki's device did not depend on piezoelectric generation alone. She combined it with triboelectric generation, which uses electrical charge produced when different materials come into contact and separate. The two mechanisms were brought together in what the project describes as a hybrid piezo–tribo nanogenerator, or HNG.Its physical arrangement was part of the experiment. The generator measured 5 by 3 centimetres and used an arch-shaped configuration, with two biomaterial-based piezoelectric sections. The eggshell membrane acted as the tribopositive base component, while mercerised cotton was positioned as the tribonegative upper section. The shape was intended to increase strain in the upper part while allowing the contact-and-separation movement needed for triboelectric generation. It was a small structure, but its design involved combining two different energy-harvesting effects rather than treating them as separate systems.The finished HNG was put through several mechanical tests to see how much electrical output it could produce. During weight-drop testing, a 1kg load was dropped from a height of 3cm at a rate of 5Hz. The generator recorded an average peak-to-peak voltage of 20.47 volts, with a variation of 2.20 volts, while its root mean square voltage was measured at 6.82 volts.The device was also tested using finger tapping, bringing the experiment closer to the kind of repeated movement that a small wearable or portable system might experience. Under forceful tapping of roughly 10 newtons at 3Hz, the HNG produced a peak output of 33.29 volts. Its reported power density reached 26.4 microwatts per square centimetre when connected to a 5-megaohm load. These measurements gave Addanki a way to compare the performance of the finished hybrid device with the individual biomaterial-based components tested earlier.The project grew out of a practical limitation in mechanical energy harvesting. Piezoelectric generators can produce electricity from deformation or movement, but some established versions rely on materials such as lead zirconate titanate, or PZT. PZT is toxic and brittle. Triboelectric generators offer another route, although their performance can be affected by environmental conditions and their electrical output can be limited depending on the materials and design.Addanki's approach was to investigate whether natural materials could form part of a different kind of generator without giving up useful electrical performance. The resulting device was not presented as a replacement for large-scale power generation. Its intended relevance was much smaller: portable electronics, wearable technology and other self-powered systems that need modest amounts of energy generated from movement. At ISEF 2025, the work appeared under the Energy: Sustainable Materials and Design category, linking the material choice with the broader question of how everyday biological materials might be used in energy-harvesting technology.
Article Summary: Eggshell membrane and mercerised cotton form a 5 by 3 centimetre hybrid nanogenerator. New Jersey high school student Meghana Addanki used both in an experiment designed to turn ordinary movement into usable electrical energy. She developed a small hybrid generator with the help of zinc oxide.

Article Title: Meet Archishman Dey, the Ohio eighth-grader who tested an air fryer, candle, humidifier, gas and incense; incense produced the most fine-particle pollution
Article Text:
Ohio eighth-grader Archishman Dey’s experiment reveals incense produced the highest PM2.5 pollution among five household sources. (Photo: Society for Science)

Archishman Dey explains why he studied indoor air pollution

He tested five common household pollution sources

Incense generated the highest PM2.5 levels

‘Everyday activities can quietly fill our lungs’

Archishman hopes to become an environmental engineer

An eighth-grader from Solon, Ohio, is drawing attention to an often-overlooked source of air pollution - the air inside our homes. Archishman Dey, a student at Solon Middle School, conducted a science project examining how common household activities affect levels of PM2.5, or fine particulate matter measuring 2.5 micrometres or less in diameter.His experiment tested five everyday sources - an air fryer, candle, humidifier, natural gas and incense. Of these, burning an incense stick produced the highest level of PM2.5 in his experiment.Archishman said his project was inspired by his concern about the air people breathe inside their homes.“When people think about air pollution, they usually imagine cars, factories, or smoke stacks outdoors, which we classify as ambient air pollution. But what if I told you that the air in your kitchen, right inside of your home, can sometimes be more polluted than the air outside?” he said in his project video.He explained that PM2.5 refers to extremely small particles that can be generated by smoke, fumes and dust from everyday activities.“PM2.5 means particulate matter. Matter less than 2.5 micrometers in diameter. So tiny that it's invisible to the naked eye,” Archishman said.He added, “These particles can go deep into our lungs and cause a variety of health issues.”According to the data published by Society for Science, Archishman became particularly interested in incense after noticing visible smoke at his grandparents’ home. His grandparents have asthma, which made him concerned about their exposure to indoor pollution.“I was most curious about the daily burning of incense sticks at my grandparents’ home, where you could visibly see smog in the air,” he said.To conduct the experiment, Archishman used an air-quality sensor to measure PM2.5 levels. He designated one room as a control area and measured the baseline concentration before testing each source.“I started wondering which activities inside of our homes produce the most of these tiny particles. That's how I came up with my project to compare five different sources of indoor PM2.5 which we use in everyday life and find out which one can pollute our indoor homes the most,” he explained.The five sources he tested were cooking on a gas stove, frying food with an air fryer, burning incense sticks, using a humidifier and burning a candle.“For each one, I measured the PM2.5 before, during, and after the activity right here in my control room to see how high the pollution levels went and how long it took to return to normal,” he said.The results showed that incense was by far the biggest source of fine-particle pollution among the five activities tested.“When I burn an incense stick, the monitor number shot up the furthest. That was the worst source by far,” Archishman said.According to the data published by Society for Science, the incense stick generated an average PM2.5 concentration of 76.27 micrograms per cubic metre. The air fryer ranked second at 14.29 micrograms per cubic metre, while the humidifier produced about 5.5 micrograms per cubic metre.Archishman said cooking on a gas stove also resulted in a significant increase in PM2.5, while burning a candle produced the smallest effect in his experiment, although it still caused a short-term spike.“The air fryer came next, followed by cooking on a gas stove, which also made for a significant increase in PM2.5. After that was using a humidifier, which only caused a small increase. Finally, burning a candle had the least effect, but there was still a short spike in PM2.5 levels,” he said.Archishman said the findings made him more aware of the pollution generated by routine household activities.“It means that everyday activities like frying food or lighting candles can quietly fill our lungs with these particles that harm our lungs,” he said.He added, “We experience this kind of exposure all the time, but most of us don't realize how slowly and steadily we're breathing these particles in.”For Archishman, the project was also about finding practical ways for families to improve their indoor environment.“I aimed to provide simple data that could enable families to recognize invisible air quality dangers and adopt healthier practices with the aim of improving their indoor environment,” he said, according to Society for Science.In his video, he suggested simple measures such as opening windows, using exhaust fans while cooking and turning on an air purifier.“The good news is that it's something we can control. By simply opening windows, using exhaust fans while cooking, or turning on an air purifier, we can reduce these pollutants within just a few minutes and make our indoor air much cleaner,” he said.Beyond the project, Archishman takes part in academic competitions including Science Olympiad and MathCounts. He has also represented Ohio at the national competition.“Cracking the code to a problem after tireless thought is what I find most enjoyable,” he said.Archishman said he hopes to become an environmental engineer and use science and mathematics to tackle major environmental challenges.“The mathematics and science behind everything around us is truly fascinating. I want to learn about these systems and solve the world's most pressing problems such as waste management, pollution and ensure a healthier planet for the future generations,” he said.He concluded his presentation with a simple message: “Even though we can't see these particles, they affect our health every day. Remember, clean air starts right here at home.”
Article Summary: Ohio eighth-grader Archishman Dey’s experiment reveals incense produced the highest PM2.5 pollution among five household sources. The air in your kitchen, right inside of your home, can sometimes be more polluted than the air outside.

Article Title: 'I don’t feel rooted here': Indian couple in Ireland to return to Pune after 11 years, citing AI pressure and job stress
Article Text:
NRI couple in Ireland for 11 years to move back to Pune and raise daughters with grandparents.

Spent 11 years in Ireland

'I don't feel rooted here'

Internet reacts

An Indian tech couple living in Ireland for more than a decade say they plan to move back to Pune by May next year, citing rising work pressure, concerns about artificial intelligence and the lack of family support while raising their two daughters.The couple shared their plans in a Reddit post, saying their children currently spend most of their day in childcare and school-related arrangements because the family has no relatives nearby.They said their routine in Ireland typically runs from 8am to 6pm, with the children moving between creche, breakfast club, school and after-school care while both parents work.“In Pune they walk out of school into their grandparents' home. This single picture does more work in my decision than any spreadsheet,” they wrote.The couple said returning to Pune would mean their daughters could spend more time with their grandparents, while the family would also have help with cooking and household chores.After 11 years in Ireland, the couple said they no longer wanted to manage work, childcare and household responsibilities without family support.They also said they were increasingly worried about the pressure created by technological and AI changes in the workplace.The couple argued that their parents' ability to spend time with their grandchildren is more valuable now than waiting another decade.“The grandparents' healthy years are now. Not in 10 years, when we'd return for hospital duty instead of daily life,” they wrote.They said their parents had previously visited Ireland for a month but found the experience difficult, making a permanent move there unrealistic.The couple also described a sense of detachment after spending more than a decade in Ireland.They said they had built a functional life there but still did not feel they had developed deep roots.“After 11 years I don't feel rooted here myself,” they said.They also described missing the everyday family and cultural connections they associate with India, arguing that celebrations and social life felt different when experienced away from their wider family.The couple said they had generally found Ireland more welcoming than the UK or US, but still felt that subtle experiences of being an outsider could affect children growing up there.Several users responded with their own experiences of living in Ireland.One user said they had moved to Ireland only recently with an infant but were already considering returning to India.“I'm in Ireland as well; I moved here recently(not even months) and am still feeling that I should move back to India. We moved here with our infant thinking it'll be better for her future, but considering the health and the daily hustle here, it feels like India would be better. She can decide for herself whether she wants to move back here or not, but we definitely are moving back within a year.”Another user said changing attitudes towards immigration could also influence people's decisions to remain in Ireland or Britain.“I would add one more reason to do so: Ireland and Britain are on a trajectory of becoming less and less welcoming to immigration. Ireland and especially the Britain that is now is not what it will be in 5 years.”A third user responded:“Wish you all the best! Good decision.”
Article Summary: Indian tech couple living in Ireland for more than a decade say they plan to move back to Pune. They cite rising work pressure, concerns about artificial intelligence and the lack of family support while raising their two daughters. The couple said returning to India would mean their daughters could spend more time with their grandparents.

Article Title: Archaeologists find earliest physical evidence of brass-making in East Asia in southern China
Article Text:
Archaeologists find the earliest physical evidence of brass-making in East Asia in southern China (PC: Cambridge University Press)

Ancient crucibles reveal early brass-making in medieval China

Ancient crucibles reveal early brass-making in medieval China (PC: AI Generated)

How did ancient craftspeople make brass from copper and zinc

How did brass-making technology reach medieval Guangzhou

What does the discovery reveal about medieval metallurgy in China

A set of ancient crucibles found in Guangzhou is giving archaeologists new clues about how brass-making technology may have reached medieval China. The vessels came from an official metallurgical workshop at the Royal Palace of the Nanyue Kingdom and dated from the ninth and tenth centuries AD. Their metal residues show that craftspeople were producing brass locally through cementation rather than simply working with imported objects. According to a research article published by Cambridge University Press, titled ‘ Brass technology transmission via maritime routes: crucible evidence from southern China ’, points towards wider technological connections with the Islamic world. Guangzhou was a major trading port, and the authors suggest maritime routes may have helped move metallurgical knowledge across regions. The study analysed crucibles using chemical, microscopic and lead-isotope methods. Together, the findings provide direct archaeological evidence for medieval brass production in southern China and offer clues about how the technology may have travelled.Archaeologists found three well-preserved brass-making crucibles at an official metallurgical workshop in Guangzhou. The workshop was part of the Royal Palace of the Nanyue Kingdom site and was active across many centuries.The three crucibles belong to the ninth–tenth century group. Each was cup-shaped with a slightly inward-sloping rim and a rounded base. Some had a pouring spout. They measured about 60-80 mm across and 60-70 mm high, with a capacity of roughly 0.2-0.3 litres. Researchers found heavy heat damage and glassy material on their surfaces. Metal residues inside included copper, zinc compounds and brass droplets. A nearby semi-subterranean furnace also dates to the seventh-tenth centuries. Together, these remains provide direct evidence of metalworking at the site.The crucial evidence came from residues left inside the crucibles. Microscopic and chemical analyses identified zinc oxide, zinc silicate, and droplets of brass. One group of crucibles contained high-purity copper and binary brass droplets with about 11-17% zinc. Another contained bronze with tin alongside zinc and produced a copper-zinc-tin alloy. The researchers interpret these residues as evidence for cementation. In this process, zinc-bearing material is heated with copper or a copper alloy so zinc enters the metal and forms brass. The remains therefore show more than the presence of finished brass objects. They preserve traces of the production process itself.The study also examined lead isotopes to investigate the likely origin of the raw materials. The three analysed crucibles had similar lead-isotope ratios that fit signatures associated with the Cathaysia tectonic province. Because these signatures occur widely across southern China, the researchers say a local source for the raw materials is reasonable. The technology itself may have travelled from farther west. The authors point to similarities between the Guangzhou crucibles and brass-making vessels associated with the Islamic world. Guangzhou was also a major international trading port. Historical evidence records connections between the city and Arab merchants. The researchers therefore suggest that maritime routes and the movement of merchants and craftsmen may have helped transmit brass-making knowledge to southern China.The findings add important evidence to the history of brass production in China. Local brass production is generally thought to have begun around the tenth century AD, but the Guangzhou crucibles provide direct evidence from the ninth-tenth centuries. The researchers argue that the discovery helps explain how a specialised metallurgical technique became established locally. It also shows why archaeological workshops can reveal details that written records alone cannot provide. The study does not claim that every element of brass technology came from one place or through one route. Instead, it highlights a possible connection between western technological traditions, maritime trade and local production in Guangzhou. The evidence adds an important piece to the history of metallurgy in East Asia.
Article Summary: Archaeologists found three well-preserved brass-making crucibles at an official metallurgical workshop in Guangzhou. The crucibles dated from the ninth and tenth centuries AD. Their metal residues show that craftspeople were producing brass locally through cementation rather than simply working with imported objects.

Article Title: Moroccan women once walked hours to collect water; now giant nets harvest drinking water from mountain fog
Article Text:
Representative Image of engineered mesh capturing fog droplets on Mount Boutmezguida for water collection (AI-generated image)

How CloudFisher nets on Mount Boutmezguida collect water from fog

Why getting Moroccan communities to accept fog water was as important as building the nets

What changed for Moroccan families once water began arriving through household taps

High on Mount Boutmezguida in southwest Morocco, more than 4,000 feet above sea level, rows of black mesh stand directly in the path of Atlantic fog rolling through the Anti-Atlas Mountains. As the fog passes through the mesh, tiny droplets collect on the fibres, run downward and are gathered before being stored and carried through pipes to homes in nearby communities. The project is operated by Dar Si Hmad, a Moroccan nonprofit whose work with fog harvesting began in 2006, initially through a pilot effort to determine whether the region's persistent coastal fog could provide a dependable source of freshwater. The later system uses CloudFisher technology developed through partnerships involving Dar Si Hmad, FogQuest and technical partners, with about 600 square metres of mesh capable of producing roughly 6,300 litres of water a day. The network now supplies five villages in the Aït Baamrane region, where reliable freshwater has historically been difficult to access. Instead of travelling long distances to wells, some households can now receive water through taps supplied by moisture collected directly from the mountain air.The technology behind the system is relatively simple in principle. Large sheets of specially engineered mesh are stretched across supporting structures in locations where dense fog regularly moves through the mountains. When moisture-laden air encounters the mesh, droplets accumulate on the fibres until gravity pulls them downward into collection gutters. The water is then channelled into reservoirs before being treated and distributed through the local network. The system at Mount Boutmezguida covers approximately 600 square metres of mesh and can produce around 6,300 litres of water per day under suitable conditions. The technology is known as CloudFisher and was developed to improve the durability and efficiency of conventional fog collectors, which have been used in different parts of the world for decades. Dar Si Hmad worked with FogQuest, a Canadian nonprofit specialising in fog and rainwater collection, as well as technical partners in developing and implementing the system. The idea itself is much older than the modern project: atmospheric moisture has been collected in various forms for centuries, but the Moroccan installation combines engineered mesh with storage, treatment and distribution infrastructure, allowing fog harvesting to function as a genuine community water supply rather than simply an experimental demonstration.The engineering was only one part of making the project work. Residents also had to become comfortable with the idea of drinking water collected directly from fog rather than water drawn from a conventional well or transported from elsewhere. A University of Toronto Reach Alliance case study examining Dar Si Hmad's work focuses heavily on this social side of the project, including community acceptance, household water management and the changes that followed once water became available closer to home. Some residents initially questioned whether fog water could provide the qualities they associated with conventional sources, while others had concerns connected to cultural and religious practices. Dar Si Hmad therefore treated community involvement as part of the infrastructure itself, working with residents to explain the system, its water treatment process and how households could conserve and maintain their new supply. The organisation also developed what it calls a water school, using the new network as an opportunity to teach communities about water management and, in some cases, literacy and numeracy. The result was that the project was not simply a set of nets installed on a mountain, but a water system that required residents to understand, trust and participate in its operation.The system's impact extends beyond the approximately 6,300 litres of water it can collect on a suitable day. Before the network was established, some families in the region depended on distant wells and had to spend significant amounts of time collecting and transporting water, a responsibility that frequently fell on women and girls. Bringing water closer to homes could therefore change how households used their time, particularly for people who had previously spent hours making water-collection trips. Dar Si Hmad's network initially supplied more than 90 households and has since been described as serving several hundred residents across five villages. The project has also demonstrated why an unconventional water source cannot be separated from the community using it: reliable collection technology matters, but so do maintenance, water education, local acceptance and an infrastructure network capable of getting the water from a mountainside to a household tap. Fog harvesting cannot solve Morocco's wider water crisis, and its output naturally depends on local fog conditions, but in the Aït Baamrane region it has transformed an atmospheric phenomenon into a practical source of freshwater. What once simply drifted over the mountains is now captured, stored, treated and delivered to people living below them.
Article Summary: Fog nets on Mount Boutmezguida collect water from the Anti-Atlas Mountains. The network now supplies five villages in the Aït Baamrane region. Instead of travelling long distances to wells, some households can now receive water through taps supplied by moisture collected directly from the mountain air.

Article Title: Canadian mom gets a complete keyboard tattooed on her arm so her autistic son can always ‘talk’ to her when his communication device fails
Article Text:
Canadian mom found a solution after her autistic son’s device died

The tattoo also gives them a private way to communicate

The keyboard idea spread beyond the family

Hunter’s friends wanted keyboard shirts too

What AAC means for non-speaking people

A dead battery led to an unexpected communication solution

A Canadian mother has found an unusual way to make sure her non-speaking autistic son always has a way to communicate with her, even when technology fails. Jessica Fletcher had a complete keyboard tattooed on her forearm after an incident with her 11-year-old son, Hunter, whose augmentative and alternative communication device ran out of battery during a meal. Hunter picked up a napkin, drew a keyboard and used it to communicate his order, giving his mother an idea for a permanent backup. Fletcher later worked with a tattoo artist to create a keyboard on her arm, complete with letters and symbols. Hunter’s first message using the tattoo was reportedly “Mama”, turning a practical solution into an emotional moment for both of them.Fletcher was eating out with Hunter when the battery on his AAC device reportedly died. The tablet allows him to select words and symbols to communicate, but without power, that option was suddenly unavailable. Hunter instead picked up a napkin, drew a keyboard on it and began pointing to the letters and symbols he needed to communicate his order. The simple workaround gave Fletcher a realisation that her son’s ability to communicate should not depend entirely on technology. She later told CTV News that the experience made her think about what would happen whenever his communication device failed.Fletcher decided to create a communication option that would never need charging. She worked with a tattoo artist to have a keyboard inked onto her forearm, allowing Hunter to tap individual letters to spell out messages. The design reportedly includes the alphabet as well as symbols such as a happy face, a sad face and an “I heart you” button. When Fletcher revealed the finished tattoo to Hunter, his first message was reportedly “Mama”. The tattoo was not intended to replace his regular AAC device. Instead, it gave him another option whenever the electronic system was unavailable.The unusual communication method has another advantage because it does not require Hunter’s messages to be spoken aloud. His electronic AAC device can produce spoken output, meaning people nearby may hear what he is communicating. By tapping letters on Fletcher’s arm, however, Hunter can communicate more quietly. The method can therefore give the mother and son a more private way to exchange messages, particularly when they are in public. Fletcher has said that removing communication barriers gives non-speaking people a greater opportunity to show others who they are and express themselves.Fletcher later posted a video of Hunter using the tattoo to communicate with her, and the clip attracted widespread attention online. The New York Post reported that she posted the video on Facebook on July 8 and that it went on to receive more than two million likes across social media. The response prompted other families and professionals to contact Fletcher about the idea. She subsequently partnered with a clothing company to create shirts featuring keyboard designs along the sleeve. Fletcher said parents, nurses, doctors and first responders from around the world had reached out about using similar ideas to help non-speaking autistic people communicate.The idea also caught the attention of Hunter’s school friends. Fletcher said some of them wanted keyboard shirts so they could communicate with him on the playground and quietly share secrets with him. The response highlights that communication is about much more than expressing basic needs. For children, it can also involve making friends, sharing jokes, discussing feelings and participating in everyday social interactions. Fletcher has said she would endure “a thousand scars” if it meant Hunter could communicate with her, underscoring how important she considers accessible communication for her son.AAC, or augmentative and alternative communication, covers a broad range of methods used by people who cannot rely on speech alone to communicate. These can include gestures, sign language, picture boards, communication books and electronic devices that produce spoken words. An electronic AAC tablet like Hunter’s is one form of this wider system. The American Speech-Language-Hearing Association describes AAC as something that can supplement speech or provide an alternative means of communication. Fletcher’s tattoo is therefore best understood as a personal, low-tech backup rather than a replacement for an established AAC system.What began with a communication device running out of power during a meal ultimately led Fletcher to create a permanent backup for her son. The keyboard tattoo gives Hunter another way to express himself when his electronic device is unavailable and can also allow him to communicate privately with his mother. Its popularity online has brought wider attention to the importance of accessible communication for non-speaking people. For Fletcher, however, the idea remains rooted in a simple goal: making sure a dead battery or technology failure does not leave her son without a way to communicate.
Article Summary: Jessica Fletcher had a complete keyboard tattooed on her forearm after an incident with her 11-year-old son, Hunter, whose augmentative and alternative communication device ran out of battery. Hunter picked up a napkin, drew a keyboard and used it to communicate his order, giving his mother an idea for a permanent backup. Fletcher later worked with a tattoo artist to create a keyboard on her arm, complete with letters and symbols. Hunter’s first message using the tattoo was reportedly “Mama”, turning a practical solution into an emotional moment for both of them.

Article Title: Meet Ishanvi Sabniveesu, the Florida 10th-grader whose AI-powered cane can describe a blind user’s surroundings, work offline and make emergency calls
Article Text:
Ishanvi Sabniveesu, the Florida 10th-grader whose AI-powered cane can describe a blind user’s surroundings (Image Credit: LinedIn/ @InventEd)

An idea born from experience

How CareCane works

It can work without internet

Emergency assistance

From STEM fair to nationals

What's next for CareCane?

Beyond visual impairment

A young inventor's approach to accessibility

For Ishanvi Sabniveesu, the idea for an assistive device began with something she had experienced herself. The Florida student, who has worn glasses since she was two, began thinking about how difficult everyday activities could be for someone with severe visual impairment. She eventually developed CareCane, an AI-powered cane designed to help visually impaired users detect obstacles, understand their surroundings and receive emergency assistance. According to FOX 13 News, which interviewed Sabniveesu about her invention, the rising junior at Steinbrenner High School won second place at the Invention Convention U.S. Nationals with CareCane.Sabniveesu's interest in helping people with visual impairments stemmed from her own experience relying on glasses. She told FOX 13 that doing simple things without her glasses had always been difficult for her, which made her consider the challenges faced by people who cannot depend on their vision. Before developing CareCane, she researched products already available on the market and visited schools for visually impaired students to gather feedback and better understand their needs.She initially considered putting similar technology into glasses.However, she realised that stability was also an important consideration for people who are blind or visually impaired. That led her to consider a cane as a more practical way to combine mobility support with technology.CareCane combines a traditional cane with built-in sensors and a camera. The sensor detects when a user is getting close to a person or object. When an obstacle is detected, the cane produces a warning beep.If the sensor continues beeping for more than five seconds, the camera automatically activates. It can then identify the user's surroundings and provide a description through connected Bluetooth speakers or headphones. The user can also activate the camera manually using a button on the cane's handle.This gives the device a function beyond simply detecting an obstacle. Instead of only indicating that something is nearby, the system is designed to provide an audio description of the surrounding environment. For someone navigating an unfamiliar setting, that additional information could potentially help them understand their surroundings without relying solely on physical contact with obstacles.One notable feature of CareCane is its ability to operate with or without internet access. Sabniveesu told FOX 13 that she deliberately designed the system this way because she wanted the device to be accessible to people in places with limited or no internet connectivity.This is particularly relevant for assistive technology because relying entirely on an internet connection could limit where a device can be used. By designing CareCane to function offline as well, Sabniveesu is attempting to make the technology useful in a wider range of circumstances.CareCane is also designed to provide an additional safety feature. Unlike some smart canes, the device includes a fall feature that can trigger emergency calls and send alerts to preset contacts through a mobile application.The feature is intended to help when a user falls and may not be able to make a call independently. Instead of functioning solely as a navigation aid, CareCane is therefore being developed as a device that combines environmental awareness with emergency communication.CareCane's journey began at the Hillsborough County STEM Fair. Sabniveesu's performance there led to an invitation to a state convention, before the invention eventually reached the national level. Earlier in June 2026, CareCane earned second place at the Invention Convention U.S. Nationals, giving Sabniveesu national recognition for the project.The award also came while the invention was still being developed, meaning the national recognition is part of an ongoing process rather than the final stage of the project.Sabniveesu is continuing to develop the device and plans to introduce additional features, including voice commands. She has also registered a startup, CareCane LLC, and has a patent pending for the device. CareCane remains in the startup-development phase, with the patent process and FDA approval still ahead.Sabniveesu's ambitions for the technology extend beyond CareCane itself. She hopes the same technology could eventually be adapted for other medical equipment, including hospital beds and wheelchairs. Her broader goal is to explore whether the technology could assist not only people with visual impairments but also people experiencing other mobility limitations.For now, CareCane remains a developing invention rather than a commercially available medical device. Its final form will depend on further development, patent processes and regulatory requirements.CareCane brings together several functions in an attempt to address everyday challenges faced by people with visual impairments. It is designed to detect nearby obstacles, describe surroundings through audio, function without constant internet access and provide emergency alerts after a fall.What makes Sabniveesu's project notable is that the invention grew from her attempt to understand a problem beyond her own experience. Rather than replacing the traditional cane, she has tried to add technology to it while preserving its role as a mobility aid.At the national convention, that idea earned her second place. As development continues, Sabniveesu is now working to turn a high school invention into a technology that could eventually provide greater information, safety and independence to people with visual and mobility challenges.
Article Summary: Ishanvi Sabniveesu, a 10th-grader at Steinbrenner High School in Florida, developed CareCane, an AI-powered cane. The device is designed to help visually impaired users detect obstacles, understand their surroundings and receive emergency assistance. It has built-in sensors and a camera that can identify the user's surroundings and provide a description through connected Bluetooth speakers or headphones.

Article Title: 'Not AI': NYC mayor Mamdani's office rejects claim over Mandarin, Bengali broadway videos
Article Text:
Mamdani rejects claims of using AI for Mandarin and Bengali videos.

New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani 's office has denied claims that artificial intelligence was used to create videos of him speaking Mandarin and Bengali while promoting the city's giveaway of 2,000 free Broadway tickets to high school students.Mamdani's press secretary and chief spokesperson, Joe Calvello, addressed the speculation on X on Sunday, writing: “And just to be clear this is NOT AI.”The mayor's office said he studied Mandarin at Bronx High School of Science, where he graduated in 2010.A spokesperson told The New York Times that Mamdani had not studied or spoken Mandarin since his school years.Queens Councilman Phil Wong, a native Mandarin speaker, also said the clip appeared genuine.“Sounds accurate. Probably rehearsed many times,” Wong told The New York Post.Mamdani also appeared in a separate video speaking Bengali, which drew attention on social media. One user commented:“I’m crying, your Bangla is better than mine.”The language videos were released as part of a city initiative offering more than 2,000 free Broadway tickets to New York City high school students.The programme, organised with the Theatre Development Fund (TDF), gives students a chance to attend one of seven Broadway shows through a free lottery.Mamdani said the scheme was intended to make New York's theatre and cultural offerings accessible to students regardless of their financial circumstances.
Article Summary: New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani's office has denied claims that artificial intelligence was used to create videos of him speaking Mandarin and Bengali. The videos were released as part of a city initiative offering more than 2,000 free Broadway tickets to New York City high school students.

Article Title: Nominee vs legal heir: What is the difference and who has claim on assets? All you need to know
Article Text:
AI image

Who is a Nominee?



Who is a Legal Heir?

Difference between a Nominee and a Legal heir

Aspect Nominee Legal Heir Role Custodian Owner Transfer of Assets Can be done without any legal formalities. Requires testamentary documents for proof of ownership. Powers No power to transact, use, or transfer assets. Power to use and transact assets as an owner. Appointment Owner can appoint anyone, but some institutions specify certain conditions. Determined by succession/personal laws. Legal Right Cannot contest ownership legally. Can contest ownership in a court of law.

When individuals open bank accounts, invest in mutual funds, or buy insurance, they are often asked to name a nominee.However, many people mistakenly assume that the nominee automatically inherits the assets. In reality, the nominee is not always the final recipient — the ownership rights belong to the legal heir, reported ET.Understanding the distinction between these two is essential to ensure that your wealth is passed on to the intended beneficiaries.A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets.The nominee’s role is limited to holding and managing the assets until they are legally transferred to the rightful heirs.According to ET, the nominee cannot sell, trade, or make any transactional decisions about the assets.The account or policy owner can appoint anyone — family, friends, or acquaintances — as a nominee, though financial institutions often prefer close family members.In some cases, the nominee and the legal heir can be the same person, which helps in ensuring a smoother transfer of assets.The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away.To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will or other testamentary proof.If there is no will — a situation known as dying intestate — the heir is determined as per the country’s succession or personal laws, reported ET.While a nominee can initially access the assets, only the legal heir can claim them permanently or challenge ownership in court.Experts quoted by ET emphasise that having clarity on this difference helps avoid disputes and ensures that the savings reach the intended family members or beneficiaries.Therefore, it is advisable to regularly update both nominees and wills to align with one’s estate planning goals.
Article Summary: A nominee acts as a temporary custodian of the deceased person’s assets. The legal heir or beneficiary is the rightful owner of the assets once the original holder passes away. To claim ownership, the legal heir must produce valid documents such as a will.
